name: Zulu
line: See the person in front of you, praise by name, work together and ask the way of those who went before.

quote.text: The way is asked of those who have gone ahead.
quote.source: Indlela ibuzwa kwabaphambili. In C. L. S. Nyembezi, Zulu Proverbs, 1954

quotes.text: A person is a person through other people.

quotes.source: Izandla ziyagezana. In C. L. S. Nyembezi, Zulu Proverbs, 1954

quotes.text: A king is a king through his people.
The bull is among the calves.
quotes.source: Inkunzi isematholeni. Tomorrow’s leaders are among today’s children

quotes.text: You will not rule when I am gone. The land will be ruled by the swallows.
quotes.source: His dying words to his assassins in 1828, according to Zulu oral tradition. The swallows are taken to mean the white settlers

words.usage: The greeting to one person. Literally we see you. Sanibonani greets more than one.
The reply to a greeting: yebo, sawubona. Yes, we see you too.

words.meaning: I am well; I am alive
words.usage: The answer to unjani, how are you. The proper reply adds a question back: and you.
From the verb bonga, which also means to praise. To thank someone is to praise them.
Said to the one who is leaving. The one who stays is told sala kahle, stay well.
The amaZulu are the people of heaven. The name comes from a founding ancestor called Zulu, who lived about 1700.

words.meaning: Humanity; being a person among persons
words.usage: Kindness, generosity and respect, understood as what makes someone fully human.
Respect shown in conduct and in speech. It includes a custom by which a married woman avoids the names of her husband’s senior relatives and words that sound like them.
The spirits of the family’s dead, who watch over the living and are spoken to at the back of the main house. Also called abaphansi, those below.
The first ancestor and creator. The word is now used for God in Zulu Christianity.
A circle of beehive houses around a cattle enclosure, home to a man, his wives, children and dependants.
The round pen at the centre of the homestead. Grain was stored in pits beneath it, and it is a place of the ancestors.
Wealth, bridewealth and the link with the ancestors. isiZulu has hundreds of terms for the colour patterns of hides.
A hereditary ruler. The Zulu king is addressed as the Lion or the Elephant.
A man appointed by the king or chief to command a regiment or administer a district.
Young men of the same age were enrolled together to serve the king as soldiers and labourers until he gave them leave to marry.

words.meaning: A matter; a discussion of it
words.usage: Business to be talked through, and the gathering at which leaders do so. The word has passed into South African English.
Poetry that names a person’s deeds, descent and character in vivid images. Kings, clans, cattle and ordinary people all have praises.
One who composes and declaims praises in public, and who may also criticise the ruler he praises.
A family name such as Zulu, Buthelezi or Khumalo. Each has its own string of praise names, called izithakazelo.
Neighbours gather to plough, weed or build for one household, which thanks them with food and beer.
Cattle, or now their value, given by the groom’s family to the bride’s. It joins two families and their ancestors.
A person called by the ancestors, most often a woman, who finds the causes of illness and misfortune.
A healer who works with plant medicines. The same word means moon and month.
Glass beads worked into panels, collars and aprons whose colours and patterns carry messages about the wearer.
Dancers in line lift one foot above the head and bring it down hard in time with the drum.
Unaccompanied male choirs with soft, careful footwork, a style born in the hostels of migrant workers. The c is a click.
A round blackened clay pot from which sorghum beer is served and shared.
A tall oval of cowhide. The colour of the hide showed the regiment.
A title of respect for any elderly woman. A grandfather is mkhulu.

practices.name: Sawubona: see the person
practices.instructions: Greet every person you meet this morning properly. Stop walking. Look at them. Say hello and ask how they are, and wait for the answer. If they ask you, answer truthfully and ask in return. Greet people you would usually pass in silence. The rule of this Onda is to greet everyone.
practices.why: Sawubona means I see you, and the reply, yebo, sawubona, means yes, I am seen. In Zulu life a person exists through being acknowledged. Greeting properly is the first courtesy.
variations: Greet in Zulu if you can.
Greet the person who cleans or serves.

practices.name: Ask the way of those ahead
practices.instructions: Think of one thing you are trying to do or decide. Find someone who has already been down that road, an older relative, a senior colleague, a neighbour, and ask them how they did it. Go in person or call. Ask, listen without arguing and thank them. Zulu proverb: ibuzwa kwabaphambili, ask of those who went before.
practices.why: Zulu culture honours those who have gone ahead, in life and in memory. Asking an elder’s advice is a mark of wisdom, not weakness.
variations: Ask a grandparent about a choice.
Ask a mentor for a story.

practices.name: Receive with both hands
practices.instructions: Today, give and receive everything with both hands, or with the right hand supported by the left at the elbow: a cup, a coin, a parcel, a document. Say thank you, ngiyabonga, as you do. In Zulu custom this shows that you value the gift and the giver. Notice how it slows and warms every small exchange.
practices.why: Receiving with both hands is a sign of gratitude and respect across Zulu and wider southern African cultures. It is a simple gesture with a big effect.

practices.name: Maize porridge breakfast
practices.instructions: Make a breakfast of maize porridge, either thick and crumbly as uphuthu or soft as isijingi, and eat it with sour milk or a little sugar. Stir it slowly in a pot as it thickens. Eat it from a bowl with a spoon, sitting down. Maize meal is the daily staple of Zulu homes. Share it with someone.
practices.why: Maize porridge in its forms is the backbone of the Zulu table. Eating it slowly at the start of the day is a plain, warming pleasure.
variations: Eat it from a shared bowl.

practices.name: Praise yourself, truthfully
practices.instructions: Compose a short praise poem about yourself, as a Zulu bard would: name your parents, your people and your place, then three things you have done and three things you are. Use images: you are the one who walks early, the one who keeps her word. Read it aloud. Izibongo are not boasting but a way of knowing who you are.
practices.why: Izibongo, praise poems, name a person’s ancestry and deeds. Every Zulu has praise names; composing yours is a strong way to start the day.

practices.name: Honour an elder
practices.instructions: Greet an older person today with special respect: stand when they come, lower your voice, let them speak first and serve them first. Hlonipha is the Zulu word for respect, shown in manner and speech. Ask how they are, offer help and listen. Avoid looking them hard in the eye.
practices.why: Hlonipha, respect for elders and in-laws, is basic to Zulu social life. It governs how one speaks, sits and serves.
variations: Carry something for an older person.
Ask an elder for a proverb.

practices.name: Praise by name
practices.instructions: Choose one person today and praise them aloud, to their face or before others. Be exact. Name what they did, what it cost and what kind of person it shows them to be, and use an image if one comes: you are the one who stood when the others sat. Say it warmly. The rule of this Onda is to praise what deserves it.
practices.why: Izibongo are given to kings and ordinary people alike. Naming a person’s qualities in front of others builds them up and builds the community.
variations: Praise a colleague in a meeting.
Praise a child for an effort.

practices.name: Join a work party
practices.instructions: Give half an hour of your labour to someone else’s job today, or call others to help with one of yours. Dig, carry, paint, cook, sort, mend. Work alongside each other and sing or talk as you go. The one who is helped feeds the helpers, with something simple and shared. The Zulu word is ilima, a work party. The rule of this Onda is to work together.
practices.why: Ilima is the call to neighbours to help with ploughing or building, repaid with food and later with return help. It is mutual aid at its best.
variations: Help a neighbour with a chore.
Call friends to help you move something.

practices.name: String a few beads
practices.instructions: Make a simple beaded bracelet or small piece of beadwork: choose seed beads, thread them on a fine thread or wire in a pattern and tie off. In Zulu beadwork, colours and patterns carry messages, such as white for purity and red for love or anger. Make one for yourself or for a friend. Take your time with the pattern.
practices.why: Zulu beadwork, ubuhlalu, is among the most famous of African crafts, with a complex code of colour. A simple bracelet is a modest start.
variations: Make a bracelet for a friend.

practices.name: A game of umlabalaba
practices.instructions: Play umlabalaba, the southern African three-in-a-row game also called morabaraba. Draw the board of three nested squares joined by lines, give each player twelve pieces and place them in turns, forming mills of three to remove opponents’ pieces. Play two games with a friend and talk as you play.
practices.why: Umlabalaba is a Zulu board game, ancient and popular, played on boards scratched in earth or drawn on paper. It is a social pastime.
variations: Play with pebbles and bottle caps.

practices.name: Skip together
practices.instructions: Skip rope with friends: two people swing a long rope and one or more jump in, chanting a rhyme or a song, as Zulu girls and boys play ingqathu. Take turns, keep the rhythm and sing. Warm up first and wear comfortable shoes. A few minutes is a good workout and great fun.
practices.why: Ingqathu is a Zulu skipping game, with songs and rhythm. It is good exercise and a happy way to spend a break.

practices.name: Walk someone to the gate
practices.instructions: When a guest leaves your home or workplace today, walk them to the gate or the door and wish them a good journey: hamba kahle, go well. The one who stays says: sala kahle, stay well. Wait until they are out of sight and wave. It is a small ritual of respect.
practices.why: Hamba kahle and sala kahle are the paired farewells of Zulu life. Walking a guest out is a sign that they mattered.

practices.name: Sing together in the evening
practices.instructions: When the day’s work is done, sing with other people. Any song that everyone knows will do. Let one voice lead and the others answer. Add a low part and a high part if you can, and move your feet in time. If you are alone, sing along to a recording. Singing in harmony is a Zulu gift.
practices.why: Zulu choral singing in four-part harmony is world-famous, from church choirs to the isicathamiya of Ladysmith Black Mambazo. Singing together is the heart of community.

practices.name: Hold an indaba
practices.instructions: Hold an indaba, a council talk, about one matter on your mind with the people it concerns. Sit in a circle. Let every person speak in turn without interruption, from the youngest to the eldest or the other way round. Seek agreement, not victory. End when there is a decision or a clear next step. Thank everyone for coming.
practices.why: An indaba is a meeting of the community to discuss and resolve matters, with respect for all voices. It is a model of consultation.

practices.name: A story from gogo
practices.instructions: Tell or read a Zulu folktale to someone, in the voice of a grandmother, gogo: begin with a call such as cosu cosu, answer iyoh, and tell of Hlakanyana the clever trickster child, or the story of the monster Isitimela. Use voices and gestures and stop at the best moment. Ask the listeners what they think happens.
practices.why: Folktales are told by grandmothers in the evening with call-and-response and songs. They teach and delight.
variations: Add a song to the story.

practices.name: Listen to isicathamiya
practices.instructions: Play Ladysmith Black Mambazo’s Shaka Zulu or another isicathamiya recording, the soft-footed a cappella harmony of Zulu miners’ choirs. Close your eyes and let the voices flow. Isicathamiya comes from cothama, to walk softly. Hum the bass line. The group sang with Paul Simon on Graceland.
practices.why: Isicathamiya was born among Zulu migrant workers in Johannesburg’s hostels in the 1930s and is sung on Saturday nights. It is both tender and rhythmic.
variations: Look up how a choir competition works.

practices.name: Remember those who came before
practices.instructions: Before bed, name the people of your family who have died, and say one thing about each. In Zulu belief the ancestors, amadlozi, remain close and are remembered in daily life. Think of what they gave you. Say thank you quietly. If you have no names to name, think of those who have helped shape your life. The rule of this Onda is to remember those who came before.
practices.why: Remembering the ancestors is central in Zulu life, and respect for them guides daily conduct. A moment of remembrance gives roots.
variations: Tell one story about a grandparent.

practices.name: Stomp a dance
practices.instructions: Put on music with a strong beat and stomp a simple dance: lift your knee high and bring your foot down hard, left, right, left, right, with arms swinging, as in the Zulu indlamu. Dance for five minutes and then rest. Do not perform a ceremonial dance; just enjoy the rhythm and the feeling of the ground. Stay within your fitness and wear shoes you can stamp in.
practices.why: Indlamu is the Zulu war and wedding dance, with high kicks and stamping. A simple stomping step is a happy way to end the day.
variations: Learn the rhythm on a drum.

practices.name: A work party
practices.instructions: Hold an ilima for a neighbour, friend or community space: invite people to help with a big job such as painting a fence, clearing a plot, planting a garden or moving furniture. Work together, sing and share a pot of food at the end. The helped person provides the meal, and everyone goes home with a story. It is the way Zulu communities have always done big jobs.
practices.why: Ilima is a cornerstone of rural Zulu life. A modern work party builds friendships as well as fences.
variations: Choose a task for an elder.

practices.name: An evening of song and dance
practices.instructions: Hold an evening of singing, dancing and sharing food with friends. Teach each other songs, one from each person’s background. Stomp, clap and harmonise. Cook a big pot of porridge and stew, and serve everyone. Include elders and children. End with a farewell song. The Zulu love of song makes any gathering festive.
practices.why: Song and dance are woven into every Zulu occasion. A shared evening of music is a gift for all.

immersePlan.name: Read Zulu proverbs
immersePlan.text: Read a handful of proverbs from C. L. S. Nyembezi’s collection. Choose one to try in a conversation today.

immersePlan.name: Read from Let My People Go
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Chief Albert Luthuli’s 1962 autobiography, a Zulu Christian leader and Nobel Peace laureate. Notice his calm.

immersePlan.name: Read from Emperor Shaka the Great
immersePlan.text: Read a passage of Mazisi Kunene’s epic poem on Shaka, written in Zulu and rendered in English. Read it aloud for the rhythm.

immersePlan.name: Watch Yesterday
immersePlan.text: Watch Darrell Roodt’s 2004 film in Zulu about a rural woman who learns she has HIV and fights to see her daughter start school. It is gentle and powerful.

immersePlan.name: Watch Amandla
immersePlan.text: Watch Lee Hirsch’s 2002 documentary on how song carried South Africans through the struggle against apartheid. Sing along to a chorus.

immersePlan.name: Watch an episode of Shaka iLembe
immersePlan.text: Watch an episode of the 2023 South African series on the life of Shaka, in Zulu. Notice the setting and the dress.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Shaka Zulu
immersePlan.text: Play Ladysmith Black Mambazo’s 1987 album, produced by Paul Simon. Listen all the way through and hum the bass.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Mahlathini and the Mahotella Queens
immersePlan.text: Play the 1987 album by the king of mbaqanga, with a growling voice and sweet female harmonies. Dance in your chair.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Princess Magogo
immersePlan.text: Play the recordings of the Zulu royal, who sang and played the ugubhu bow. Listen to her voice.

immersePlan.name: Look at Zulu beadwork
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of Zulu beadwork, necklaces, belts and love letters in beads. Find a colour code online and read a piece.

immersePlan.name: Look at Zulu beer pots
immersePlan.text: Look at the black burnished pots with raised patterns made by potters such as Nesta Nala. Notice the shapes.

immersePlan.name: Look at telephone-wire baskets
immersePlan.text: Look at the brightly coloured baskets woven from discarded telephone wire. Notice how rubbish becomes beauty.

immersePlan.name: Make uphuthu with amasi
immersePlan.text: Stir maize meal into boiling water until crumbly, and serve it with soured milk. Eat with a spoon.

immersePlan.name: Make ujeqe
immersePlan.text: Steam a dough of wheat flour and yeast in a pot above water. Eat it with a stew.

immersePlan.name: Make isijingi
immersePlan.text: Cook maize meal with pumpkin into a soft, sweet porridge. Eat it warm.

immersePlan.name: Drink amasi
immersePlan.text: Drink a glass of soured milk, thick and tangy, as in rural Zulu homes. Use buttermilk or kefir if you cannot find it.

immersePlan.name: Learn about utshwala
immersePlan.text: Utshwala is sorghum beer, shared from a common pot in rural homes in set order. Read about it and drink a glass of sorghum or maize porridge drink instead.

immersePlan.name: Drink amahewu
immersePlan.text: Drink a glass of amahewu, a lightly soured maize drink, cold from the bottle or home-made. Notice its tang.

immersePlan.name: Receive with both hands
immersePlan.text: Give and receive everything with both hands today, and say thank you.

immersePlan.name: Greet by clan name
immersePlan.text: Learn about clan names, isibongo, and praise names. Greet someone with a respectful name or title today.

immersePlan.name: Show respect to an elder with your gaze
immersePlan.text: Learn why some Zulu people lower their gaze before an elder. Try gentler eye contact with an older person.

immersePlan.name: Play umlabalaba
immersePlan.text: Play the southern African three-in-a-row game on a drawn board with pebbles, forming mills to capture your friend’s pieces.

immersePlan.name: Skip together
immersePlan.text: Skip with a long rope swung by two friends and chant a rhyme or song as you jump in, taking turns.

immersePlan.name: Play amagende
immersePlan.text: Play a stone game: toss stones in the air and catch them, picking up others. Use pebbles and play with a friend.

immersePlan.name: Mark Heritage Day
immersePlan.text: Heritage Day, 24 September, is South Africa’s national day of culture, also called Braai Day. Share a meal and a story of your heritage.

immersePlan.name: Learn about the Reed Dance
immersePlan.text: Read about the Umhlanga, where thousands of young women carry reeds to the royal household in September. Respect it as a Zulu cultural event.

immersePlan.name: Look up Ondini
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of King Cetshwayo’s royal homestead at Ulundi, reconstructed with beehive huts. Imagine the daily life.

immersePlan.name: Practise sawubona
immersePlan.text: Sawubona means I see you. Greet three people today by really seeing them.

immersePlan.name: Practise ubuntu
immersePlan.text: Ubuntu means a person is a person through other persons. Do something today that you could only do with others.

immersePlan.name: Practise hlonipha
immersePlan.text: Hlonipha is respect. Show special respect to one person today.

rules.why: Stop, look and ask after them. To be seen is to exist.
Give way, speak after them and ask their guidance.
Know their names. They are still part of the family.
Say it aloud and by name. Thanks and praise are one word.
Hands wash each other. Lend yours and ask for others’.
Stand straight, keep your word and do not shame your name.

read.title: Emperor Shaka the Great: A Zulu Epic
read.creator: Mazisi Kunene
read.why: Seventeen thousand lines on the life of Shaka, composed in Zulu from oral tradition and translated by the poet. It shows a nation builder and thinker where colonial writers saw a tyrant.

read.title: Let My People Go
read.creator: Albert Luthuli
read.why: The autobiography of a Zulu chief, teacher and Christian who led the African National Congress and won the Nobel Peace Prize.

read.title: Zulu Proverbs
read.creator: C. L. S. Nyembezi
read.why: Hundreds of proverbs with translations and explanations of where each comes from, by a great scholar of the language.

read.title: Zulu Horizons
read.creator: B. W. Vilakazi, translated by Florence Louie Friedman
read.why: English versions of the poems that founded modern Zulu literature in the 1930s and 1940s.

read.title: Rope of Sand: The Rise and Fall of the Zulu Kingdom in the Nineteenth Century
read.creator: John Laband
read.why: The standard narrative history, from Shaka to the British conquest.

read.title: Terrific Majesty: The Powers of Shaka Zulu and the Limits of Historical Invention
read.creator: Carolyn Hamilton
read.why: How the image of Shaka was made and remade by Zulu and by white writers.

watch.title: Shaka iLembe
watch.creator: Mzansi Magic
watch.why: A South African series in isiZulu on the making of the Zulu king, written with historians and the royal family.

watch.title: Yesterday
watch.creator: Darrell James Roodt
watch.why: A mother in a rural village in KwaZulu-Natal learns that she is ill and sets herself to live until her daughter starts school. The first feature film in isiZulu.

watch.title: On Tiptoe: Gentle Steps to Freedom
watch.creator: Eric Simonson
watch.why: Joseph Shabalala and Ladysmith Black Mambazo, and the story of isicathamiya.

watch.title: Amandla: A Revolution in Four-Part Harmony
watch.creator: Lee Hirsch
watch.why: How song carried the struggle against apartheid.

listen.title: Shaka Zulu
listen.creator: Ladysmith Black Mambazo
listen.why: Ten men’s voices, deep and soft, from the group Joseph Shabalala formed in Ladysmith in the 1960s.

listen.title: Urbanzulu
listen.creator: Busi Mhlongo
listen.why: Maskandi, the music of Zulu guitarists and migrant workers, sung by a woman with a huge voice.

listen.title: Thokozile
listen.creator: Mahlathini and the Mahotella Queens
listen.why: Township mbaqanga: a growling bass singer, three women in harmony and a driving band.

listen.title: The Zulu Songs of Princess Constance Magogo kaDinuzulu
listen.creator: Princess Magogo, recorded by Hugh Tracey
listen.why: A king’s daughter sings old royal songs to the single-stringed musical bow.

art.title: Beadwork
art.creator: Zulu women
art.why: Small panels and necklaces given as tokens between young people. White, red, blue, green, yellow, pink and black each carry several meanings, which shift with their neighbours.

art.title: Beer pots
art.creator: Nesta Nala and the potters of the Thukela valley
art.why: Hand-coiled vessels burnished and fired black, with raised bumps in bands. Nesta Nala made the form known across the world.

art.title: Telephone wire baskets
art.creator: Zulu weavers
art.why: Night watchmen began weaving bright plastic-coated wire into bowls with spiralling patterns. It is now a major craft.

art.title: The married woman’s hat
art.creator: Isicholo
art.why: A wide flaring disc, once a hairstyle built up with red ochre and fat and later a hat of woven fibre.

eat.title: Uphuthu with amasi
eat.creator: Crumbly maize meal with soured milk
eat.why: The everyday dish. The maize is cooked dry and broken up with a fork, and the thick sour milk is poured over.

eat.title: Ujeqe
eat.creator: Steamed bread
eat.why: A soft white loaf steamed in a pot, eaten with stew or beans.

eat.title: Isijingi
eat.creator: Pumpkin and maize porridge
eat.why: Sweet, yellow and smooth. A food of autumn.

eat.title: Amadumbe
eat.creator: A small taro root
eat.why: Boiled in its skin and eaten with salt. Grown along the humid coast.

drink.title: Amasi
drink.creator: Soured milk
drink.why: Once fermented in a gourd. By custom it was shared only among relatives.

drink.title: Utshwala
drink.creator: Sorghum beer
drink.why: Brewed by the women of the house over several days. It is thick, sour and low in alcohol, and the first drops are for the ancestors.

drink.title: Amahewu
drink.creator: A fermented maize drink
drink.why: Thin, slightly sour and not alcoholic. Drunk by workers in the fields.

customs.title: Receiving with both hands
customs.creator: A sign of gratitude
customs.why: A gift is taken with both hands cupped, or with the right hand while the left touches the right forearm.

customs.title: Greeting by clan name
customs.creator: Praise names
customs.why: A person may be greeted or thanked by their clan name and its praises, which honours all their ancestors at once.

customs.title: The shared beer pot
customs.creator: Passed in order
customs.why: The host drinks first to show the beer is good, and the pot then passes by seniority. One kneels or sits to drink.

customs.title: Not looking an elder in the eye
customs.creator: Lowered gaze
customs.why: Young people show respect by not staring at their seniors and by sitting when an elder is seated.

games.title: Stick fighting
games.creator: Martial game · Zulu
games.why: Two young men fence with a striking stick and a parrying stick under the eye of a referee. A bout ends at first blood and the fighters wash each other’s wounds.

games.title: Umlabalaba
games.creator: Board game · southern Africa
games.why: Each player places and moves twelve stones, called cows, to make rows of three and take the opponent’s. Herd boys scratch the board in the earth.

games.title: Ingqathu
games.creator: Skipping · Zulu
games.why: Rope skipping with songs, by one child or many at once.

games.title: Amagende
games.creator: Stone game · Zulu
games.why: One stone is thrown up while others are scooped in and out of a hollow, in rounds of rising difficulty.

festivals.title: The Reed Dance
festivals.creator: September, Nongoma, KwaZulu-Natal
festivals.why: Umkhosi woMhlanga. Tens of thousands of young women carry tall reeds to the king’s residence. It belongs to its participants.

festivals.title: Heritage Day
festivals.creator: 24 September, KwaDukuza
festivals.why: The day once kept as Shaka’s Day. The king addresses the nation at Shaka’s grave.

festivals.title: The First Fruits
festivals.creator: December, Nongoma
festivals.why: Umkhosi Wokweshwama. The king tastes the new harvest before anyone else may, and the regiments gather.

festivals.title: The Isandlwana commemoration
festivals.creator: January, Isandlwana
festivals.why: Regiments in traditional dress and British re-enactors mark the battle of 1879 together.

places.title: Isandlwana
places.creator: KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
places.why: The sphinx-shaped hill where the Zulu army destroyed a British column on 22 January 1879. White cairns mark where the dead were buried.

places.title: The eMakhosini valley
places.creator: Near Ulundi, KwaZulu-Natal
places.why: The Valley of the Kings, where the early Zulu chiefs are buried, with the rebuilt royal residence of Dingane at uMgungundlovu.

places.title: Ondini
places.creator: Ulundi, KwaZulu-Natal
places.why: The capital of King Cetshwayo, burned by the British in 1879. Part of the great circle of houses has been rebuilt, with a museum beside it.

places.title: KwaDukuza
places.creator: North coast, KwaZulu-Natal
places.why: The site of Shaka’s last capital and of his grave, in the middle of a modern town.

places.title: Ncome
places.creator: Near Dundee, KwaZulu-Natal
places.why: A museum built in the shape of the Zulu battle formation, facing the Afrikaner monument across the river where the two armies met in 1838.

places.title: The Luthuli Museum
places.creator: Groutville, KwaZulu-Natal
places.why: The modest home of Chief Albert Luthuli, where he lived under banning orders.

ethics.title: Ubuntu
ethics.text: You become human by how you treat others.
ethics.practice: Do one kindness today for someone who cannot repay it.

ethics.title: Respect
ethics.text: Honour age, rank and the dead.
ethics.practice: Let an older person go first and speak first.

ethics.title: Courage
ethics.text: Stand firm and face what must be faced.
ethics.practice: Have the conversation you are avoiding.

ethics.title: Generosity
ethics.text: A visitor is fed. A stingy person is no person.

ethics.title: Solidarity
ethics.practice: Help with a job that is not yours.

ethics.title: Dignity
ethics.text: Bear yourself well and keep your name clean.
ethics.practice: Do nothing today that you would not want told of you.

philosophy.title: A person through people
philosophy.text: No one becomes a person alone. Character is made in relationships and shown in them.
philosophy.practice: Who made you who you are?

philosophy.title: To see and be seen
philosophy.text: The greeting says we see you. Recognition is the first gift.

philosophy.title: The living and the dead
philosophy.text: The ancestors are part of the family and take an interest in it.
philosophy.practice: What would your dead say about how you are living?

philosophy.title: The king through the people
philosophy.text: Authority exists because people give it and can be forfeited by misuse.
philosophy.practice: What authority do you hold, and who gave it?

philosophy.title: Praise as truth
philosophy.text: A praise names what a person really is. It can also contain a rebuke.
philosophy.practice: What would an honest praise poem say of you?

philosophy.title: The one who went ahead
philosophy.text: Wisdom is experience passed down, not invented afresh.

philosophy.title: Cattle as relationship
philosophy.text: Cattle joined families in marriage and the living with the dead. Wealth was a tie, not a hoard.
philosophy.practice: What do you own that binds you to others?

philosophy.title: Whose Shaka
philosophy.text: Much of what is told about the Zulu past was written by their enemies.
philosophy.practice: Who wrote the story you believe about yourself?

intro: The Zulu are the largest people of South Africa. About thirteen million strong, they make up nearly a quarter of the population, and isiZulu is the most widely spoken home language in the country. Their heartland is the province of KwaZulu-Natal, a country of green hills that falls from the Drakensberg mountains to the Indian Ocean, though millions also live in and around Johannesburg.

They belong to the Nguni branch of the Bantu-speaking peoples, farmers and cattle keepers who have lived in south-eastern Africa for well over a thousand years. Until about two hundred years ago the Zulu were one small clan among many, named after a founding ancestor, Zulu, whose name means heaven. In 1816 Shaka, a son of the Zulu chief, took the chieftainship. Within a dozen years, by war, diplomacy and the absorbing of defeated neighbours, he had built a kingdom of perhaps a quarter of a million people. Its strength lay in the regiments, into which all the young men of the kingdom were enrolled by age, and which served the king as army and workforce.

Life was centred on the homestead, a circle of domed thatched houses around a cattle enclosure. Cattle were the measure of wealth, the means of marriage and the link with the ancestors, who remained members of the family and were spoken to and given offerings. Manners rested on respect for seniors. History, law and identity were carried in speech, above all in praise poetry, which records the deeds of kings and clans in compressed and brilliant images.

The kingdom met the expanding European colonies almost at once. Shaka was assassinated by his half-brothers in 1828. His successor Dingane fought the Afrikaner trekkers and was defeated at the Ncome river in 1838. In January 1879 Britain invaded. At Isandlwana the army of King Cetshwayo overran a British camp, among the worst defeats ever inflicted on a colonial force, but by July the capital was burned, the king was a prisoner and the kingdom had been broken into thirteen pieces. A last armed rising against a poll tax, led by Chief Bhambatha, was crushed in 1906.

Under segregation and apartheid the Zulu lost most of their land and became a reservoir of migrant labour for the mines and cities. In those hostels and townships new music was born, and Zulu leaders stood at the head of the freedom struggle: John Dube was the first president of the African National Congress and Albert Luthuli its president when he won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1960. The years before the first democratic election in 1994 brought bitter political violence in the province.

Today the Zulu king has no political power and great symbolic weight. The language thrives in radio, television, music and literature. Most Zulu are Christians, many in African independent churches, and respect for the ancestors continues beside it.
This Onda takes its practices from everyday Zulu manners and arts: the greeting, asking the way, praise, the work party and song.
guide.origin: KwaZulu-Natal, on the eastern coast of South Africa
guide.era: The Zulu clan dates from about 1700 and the kingdom from 1816. Some thirteen million people are Zulu today

figures.name: Mkabayi kaJama
figures.bio: A princess who never married, ruled as regent and decided the succession more than once. She had a hand in the removal of Shaka and of Dingane.

figures.name: Nandi
figures.bio: The mother of Shaka, who raised him in exile and hardship. As queen mother she was among the most powerful people in the kingdom.

figures.name: Shaka kaSenzangakhona
figures.bio: The founder of the Zulu kingdom. A commander of genius and a ruthless ruler, known chiefly through oral tradition and the accounts of a few traders.

figures.name: Cetshwayo kaMpande
figures.bio: The king who tried to avoid war with Britain, won at Isandlwana, lost his kingdom and travelled to London to plead with Queen Victoria for its return.

figures.name: Bhambatha kaMancinza
figures.bio: A chief of the Zondi who led the last armed resistance to colonial rule in Natal.

figures.name: Dinuzulu kaCetshwayo
figures.bio: Cetshwayo’s heir, exiled to Saint Helena for seven years and later imprisoned for his supposed part in the rising of 1906.

figures.name: John Langalibalele Dube
figures.bio: Minister, educator and newspaper founder. He set up the Ohlange Institute in 1900 and was the first president of the African National Congress in 1912.

figures.name: Albert Luthuli
figures.bio: Teacher, elected chief of Groutville and president of the African National Congress. He was the first African to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.

figures.name: Princess Magogo kaDinuzulu
figures.bio: Singer, composer and player of the musical bow, who preserved a great body of royal song.

figures.name: Benedict Wallet Vilakazi
figures.bio: Poet, novelist and the first Black South African to earn a doctorate. He brought new forms into Zulu verse.

figures.name: Mazisi Kunene
figures.bio: Poet of two great epics in isiZulu, written in exile. South Africa’s first poet laureate.

figures.name: Joseph Shabalala
figures.bio: A farm boy from Ladysmith who dreamed a sound, founded Ladysmith Black Mambazo and took Zulu harmony around the world.

history.detail: Bantu-speaking communities who grow grain, keep cattle and work iron are settled in what is now KwaZulu-Natal.
Zulu, son of Malandela, founds a small chiefdom in the valley of the White Mfolozi.
On the death of his father Senzangakhona, Shaka takes the chieftainship with the backing of his patron Dingiswayo.
Shaka defeats the Ndwandwe and brings the chiefdoms between the Phongolo and the Thukela under one rule. The upheavals of these years scatter peoples across southern Africa.
Shaka is stabbed at KwaDukuza by his half-brothers Dingane and Mhlangana. Dingane takes the throne.
Dingane has the Boer leader Piet Retief and his party killed in February. On 16 December a Boer force defeats the Zulu army at the Ncome, which they name Blood River.
Dingane’s brother rules for thirty-two years in uneasy peace with the colony of Natal. His sons fight a civil war in 1856, which Cetshwayo wins.
Some twenty thousand Zulu overwhelm the British camp. About thirteen hundred of the invading force are killed, and more than a thousand Zulu.
The British defeat the Zulu army and burn the capital. The kingdom is divided among thirteen appointed chiefs and falls into civil war.
Britain annexes Zululand and then joins it to Natal. Much of the land is opened to white farmers.
A poll tax provokes rebellion. Colonial troops kill between three and four thousand people.
John Dube is elected first president of what becomes the African National Congress. The Natives Land Act reserves most of the country for whites.
A KwaZulu homeland is set up under Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi. Conflict between his Inkatha movement and supporters of the African National Congress costs many thousands of lives.
KwaZulu-Natal becomes a province of a democratic South Africa. King Goodwill Zwelithini reigns for fifty years until 2021 and is succeeded by Misuzulu kaZwelithini.

concepts.detail: A person’s worth and identity come from their relationships. The proverb about being a person through people is Zulu in the form most often quoted.
A code of deference toward seniors, in-laws and the ancestors, with its own vocabulary of avoidance.
They protect, warn through dreams and illness, and are addressed with offerings of beer and meat at family ceremonies.
Age regiments cut across clan loyalties and bound young men directly to the king. They built his residences, herded his cattle and fought his wars.
The layout shows the order of the family: the great house at the top, the wives’ houses by rank on either side and the enclosure of the cattle and ancestors in the middle.
Izibongo are built from praise names strung together. They are a people’s archive and are still composed for presidents, kings and footballers.
Ilobolo is negotiated between families and creates lasting obligations on both sides. It is not a purchase.
The king embodied the unity of the people and led the great rituals of the first fruits. He ruled with a council and through chiefs.
Historians debate how far the upheavals of Shaka’s time were caused by the Zulu kingdom and how far by drought and the slave and ivory trades.

facts.text: isiZulu has three click sounds, written c, q and x, which it took from the Khoisan languages.
The battle formation credited to Shaka was called the horns of the buffalo: a chest, two encircling horns and a reserve of loins.
The song that became The Lion Sleeps Tonight was composed in isiZulu by Solomon Linda in 1939 under the title Mbube, lion.
The South African national anthem includes a verse in isiZulu.
Words such as indaba, impi and donga have entered South African English from isiZulu.
Nelson Mandela cast his first vote, in 1994, at John Dube’s Ohlange school.

sensitivity.note: The Zulu are a living nation of some thirteen million people. This Onda was written by outsiders from published sources and borrows only everyday manners and arts. It should be reviewed by Zulu readers.
requiredCaveats: The picture of the Zulu as a warrior people was largely made by their colonial enemies. Much of what is told of Shaka comes from hostile or self-interested witnesses.
Ceremonies for the ancestors, the calling of a diviner, the Reed Dance and the First Fruits belong to Zulu families and the Zulu nation. Nothing here asks you to imitate them.
Some customs described, such as hlonipha speech and bridewealth, are debated among Zulu people today, particularly by women.
Pronunciations are approximate. The clicks and the hl and dl sounds of isiZulu cannot be shown in English spelling.
